A content delivery network exists to make websites and videos load quickly no matter where a person happens to be. Every website lives somewhere specific, on a machine called an origin server — the original computer that stores the real, complete version of a site's files. If every single request had to travel all the way to that one machine, people far away would face frustrating delays. So instead, copies of the content get stored on many computers scattered around the world, positioned close to where people actually are; each of those nearby computers is called an edge location. When someone requests a page, the network first checks whether a nearby edge location already has a saved copy — if it does, that's called a cache hit, meaning the answer can be delivered instantly without bothering the distant origin server at all. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood bakeries that all sell bread baked from the same recipe at one central kitchen, so nobody has to drive across the country just for a loaf. This setup reduces waiting time, eases strain on the original server, and keeps things running smoothly even when many people request the same content at once.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer holding the real, master copy of a website's content | Everything ultimately traces back here if no nearby copy exists |
| Edge location | A nearby computer holding a stored copy of the content | Being physically closer means much faster delivery |
| Cache hit | When a nearby copy successfully answers a request | Saves time and avoids unnecessary trips to the origin server |
| Latency | The delay between asking for something and receiving it | Shorter delay means a smoother, more enjoyable experience |
